Investment memo · Medartis Holding AG (MED-CH)

Medartis: a protected, predictable revenue engine inside a company with unpredictable earnings, and the brokers' EPS is likely to reset on 2 March 2027, before the earnings case can be proven

19 November 2026. Share price CHF 109.00 (13 November 2026). Money in CHF millions unless stated; per-share figures in CHF. Notes on the numbers are at the end.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in one picture. Medartis is a protected product, like Bonesupport's, inside a company built like Medacta, a Swiss orthopaedic grower. The product is TOUCH, a thumb-base joint replacement with US approval, a three-year Medicare payment window and no rival. The company around TOUCH has Swiss-franc costs, places instrument sets at its own expense, and consumes cash as it grows. TOUCH makes Medartis's revenue unusually predictable. The company's cost structure makes Medartis's earnings unusually hard to predict. The share price pays for both to go right.

The eight things that matter.

  1. Medartis offers two forecasts of very different quality. The 80% range for FY2027 revenue is about 4% either side of the model. The 80% range for FY2027 EPS runs from 38% below the model to 44% above it. Treat revenue and EPS as separate bets.
  2. The positive skew is in growth guidance; the negative skew is in the brokers' EPS. Richard's test is whether fundamental outcomes and the odds of upgrades are unusually skewed to the positive. On growth guidance, the skew is positive. On the EPS of the two brokers (UBS and Stifel, the only contributors FactSet shows), the skew is negative for the next two results. The case therefore fails the test today, and could pass it once the brokers' numbers have reset.
  3. The first reset has a date: 2 March 2027. The model agrees with the two brokers' FY2026 figures down to pre-tax profit, so the whole FY2026 EPS gap is one line, tax. I expect the FY2026 results to show a growth beat and an earnings miss on the same morning.
  4. The earnings step-up is real, back-loaded and conditional. The model takes EPS from CHF 1.23 in FY2026 to CHF 3.20 in FY2029. In FY2027, however, revenue growth alone adds only about CHF 0.05 of EPS. Nearly 90% of the FY2027 rise in EPS needs a higher margin and a lower tax rate, and Medartis has demonstrated neither.
  5. At the guideline fair multiple, the model shows a total return of +62.7% to end-2027 and +121.4% to mid-2029. Almost all of each return is earnings growth at a held multiple. In my view the guideline multiple is the top of the defensible range, not its centre. The 18-month return is therefore a judgement about the multiple. The three-year return is a judgement about earnings, and it survives a severe de-rating.
  6. Three of my readings differ from the earlier analysts' work. First, the change of US leadership lies ahead (1 January 2027), not behind. Second, the stock did not "look through" the March 2026 earnings miss; it fell about 17% that month. Third, TOUCH volume has upside the model does not need, while TOUCH's price, which nobody can verify, matters more than its volume.
  7. Five judgements move the shares: US TOUCH volume and price; growth outside TOUCH in the first year of hard comparisons; how much margin management releases; the tax rate; and the Swiss franc. Topic #6 gives the arithmetic for each.
  8. The risks are dated, countable and mostly non-fatal. The earnings-side risks do not damage the franchise. The franchise-side risks (a TOUCH safety signal, a payment change, a rival) are low-probability and can be monitored in public device databases and Medicare rules.

The sequence to hold in mind: the case is decided on a short list of dated events, and the first, the FY2026 results on 2 March 2027, fixes the most. Those results fix the FY2026 tax charge, the margin wording for FY2027, the TOUCH exit rate and the debt position.

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the headwinds against them

Conclusion: the external environment is a dated, narrow and real tailwind for revenue through 2028, and close to neutral for earnings.

Evidence: three forces work for Medartis, and each has a date.

  • A payment decision has created a US market for TOUCH. TOUCH received US premarket approval in July 2025 with its own procedure code, and Medicare makes a pass-through payment for it from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2028. The pass-through pays the hospital for the device on top of the procedure. The pathway TOUCH used closed to new applicants after 1 October 2026, and no rival US thumb-base prosthesis is in sight. Australia listed TOUCH for reimbursement from 1 July 2026. In the sector, revenue typically follows a payment decision by about a year, which puts TOUCH's largest effect in 2027.
  • The end market is the fastest-growing corner of orthopaedics. Extremities grow about 9% a year, against 3% to 5% for general orthopaedics, and hand and trauma surgery cannot be deferred for long.
  • Tariffs are being engineered away. Medartis will make 70% of its US volume in Warsaw, Indiana by end-2026 and about 80% by mid-2027. Tariff refunds already cut the 2026 charge, so the margin gain in 2027 is small: 0.3 to 0.5 points.

Smaller tailwinds: Australia's price cuts ended in July 2025, EU device rules are easing, and rivals are absorbed in their own reorganisations (DePuy Synthes is to be separated by mid-2027; Zimmer Biomet is absorbing Paragon 28).

Evidence: four forces work against Medartis.

  • The Swiss franc, unhedged by policy. In FY2025 the franc took 4.4 points off reported growth and about 1.2 points off the margin. The franc bites on reported earnings, which is where the stock is weakest.
  • US elective demand has softened, but not for protected products. Medacta warned on 5 November 2026 of insurers refusing pre-authorisation and of higher patient deductibles; Treace's Q3 revenue fell 4%; Stryker, Globus and Smith & Nephew cut their 2026 guidance. In the same quarter Paragon 28 grew 18% and Bonesupport's US sales grew 49%: protected products early in their adoption held up, and mature elective lines did not.
  • Competition is rising in product, not in price. Acumed made three moves in hand and wrist within three months, and Stryker's Pangea plating system has reached Europe, Medartis's home market.
  • The hospital administrator, not the surgeon, is the gate. Hospital value-analysis committees take up to four months per hospital to approve a product.

Inference: the tailwinds act on revenue, not on margin. The tailwinds are narrow, dated and strong enough to carry high-teens organic growth through 2027. None of them delivers margin: the tariff gain is small, and the franc can take it back.

So what. 2027 and 2028 sit inside a protected window that few small medical-device companies ever get: approval, payment, no rival, and the regulatory door closed behind TOUCH. The window also has an end date: a Medicare rule proposed in mid-2028 will set TOUCH's payment for 2029.

Strongest counter-case: insurers could pause TOUCH. A thumb-base replacement is an elective operation, and its typical patient is an older woman facing a deductible. If insurers' refusals spread from hips and knees to hand surgery in the first year of hard comparisons, TOUCH adoption could pause, as Bonesupport's product did in Q2 2026. A one-quarter pause in TOUCH is worth three to four points of group growth in a half-year.

What would change my view. A flat TOUCH run-rate at the March 2027 update; a change to TOUCH's procedure code or payment group in the 2028 outpatient rule (proposed about July 2027); a rival's US filing; a sharp fall in the dollar against the franc.

Against the market. The prevailing narrative treats Medartis as the exception to US elective weakness because TOUCH has no rival. I agree for 2027, and the Q3 2026 split supports that view. I differ in two places. Having no rival protects TOUCH's share and price, but not its volume against an insurer's refusal. And nobody is yet discussing the 2029 payment reset, which lies outside the 18-month window but inside the three-year one.

68

Score: 68, set by the Rater. Enacted, dated external forces lift revenue: US approval with its own code and Medicare pass-through payment for TOUCH to end-2028, with the pathway closed behind it, Australian listing, extremities growing about 9% a year against 3-5% for orthopaedics, and tariffs engineered away. Net of the direct threats (unhedged franc, softer US elective demand, Acumed and Stryker in product), they add materially to organic growth through 2028 but almost nothing to margin, and reach a protected product that is about 9% of FY2027 sales plus a growing niche. That is a clear positive below the multi-part 75s, coherent with the group's 65; I sit just below Eckert & Ziegler, whose regulated structural demand is similar but broader, and above Linea Directa's advanced pricing cycle.

#2 Internally driven corporate change, and its problems

Conclusion: corporate change is strong, fast and proven on growth, unproven on profit and cash, and about to be tested by a leadership gap in its most important region.

Evidence: almost everything at Medartis has changed in 24 months, and the change shows in the growth numbers.

  • People. Chief executive Matthias Schupp arrived in November 2024 after 17 years at Straumann, where he built the Neodent value brand. Finance director Dr Peter Hackel, formerly Straumann's finance director, arrived in January 2026 with a mandate to improve cash conversion.
  • Actions. Medartis replaced about 20 of its 57 US distribution partners within months, including its largest Florida distributor (nearly 10% of US sales). It bought the rest of KeriMedical, TOUCH's maker, for CHF 99m in the month US approval arrived. It bought NeoOrtho (Brazilian value implants) and integrated it in ten months. It moved US-bound production within weeks of the tariff spike. It bought a surgical-education centre in Miami and is training 330 US hand surgeons in 2026.
  • Incentives. The annual bonus is weighted 50% to sales growth, 30% to the operating-cost ratio and 20% to EBITDA margin. Long-term awards now depend on relative shareholder return and a cash-flow measure.
  • Results. Organic growth has stepped up for two years, to 27.4% in the US in H1 2026 (chart below). Exclusive US distributors grew 46%, against 16% for multi-line distributors.

Three qualifications matter.

  1. The US leadership change is ahead of us, not behind us. The earlier work treated the slide stating that "the finance director is US head ad interim as of January 2027" as mis-dated. I read the slide as forward-dated. Three separate readings of the H1 2026 results presentation in our research give the same date, and the AlphaSense report states that David Thoni, US President since January 2025, stays until the end of 2026 and that Dr Hackel takes the US role ad interim from 1 January 2027. No press release confirms the change and no successor is named, so I put its probability at about 70%. Two consequences follow. First, the US growth of H1 2026 was earned with a US President in post, so it does not show that the US business runs well without one. Second, the executive whose mandate is cash, margin and tax takes on a second job in the year those three are due to deliver. Latin America also has no permanent head.
  2. The demonstrated US strength is mostly TOUCH. US sales grew 27.4% in H1 2026, an increase of about CHF 6.5m at constant currency. Roughly 900 TOUCH procedures account for CHF 3m to 4.7m of that increase, depending on TOUCH's price, which leaves US growth outside TOUCH at about 7% to 14%. Management describes plate sales into TOUCH accounts as "still building", and South Florida has not fully recovered from the distributor change. The rebuilt US plating channel has not yet shown the 20%-plus growth that the US ambition assumes.
  3. The change has been paid for from the balance sheet. Cash fell by CHF 113m in eighteen months and bank loans rose by about CHF 26m in six (chart above). Six programmes run at once; "we have some balls in the air", says the chief executive. The founder sold 3.4% of his holding in 2025, while the chief executive bought shares.

Inference: the first half of the change, growth, is proven; the second half, profit, has not begun to show. Medartis is a genuine corporate-change case. Turning growth into operating margin, cash and returns has not yet started: the core EBIT margin is still about 9%.

So what. The change forces justify trusting management's operating targets. They do not yet justify trusting the profit conversion that the brokers' numbers and the share price assume.

Strongest counter-case: profit conversion may be the next chapter of the Straumann playbook. This team learned its trade at Straumann, which converted share gains into margin through scale, and Medartis's pay now rewards the cost ratio and cash. Putting the finance director in charge of the US may be how management imposes cost discipline where the money is being spent.

What would change my view. Up: a permanent US President with large-company experience named before or with the March 2027 results. Down: the US seat still filled ad interim at the August 2027 results; another acquisition funded with debt.

Against the market. The narrative treats the transformation as done and working. I agree on growth. I think the market has not registered two things: that the US seat changes hands on 1 January 2027, in the first year of hard comparisons, and how much of US growth comes from one product.

73

Score: 73, set by the Rater. A broad, fast reset already in the numbers on growth: new Straumann-trained CEO and CFO, about 20 of 57 US distributors replaced, KeriMedical bought and NeoOrtho integrated, production moved, 330 surgeons trained, and organic growth up from 11.7% to 15.7% to 17.0% (US +27.4%). It is held back because the profit, cash and tax outputs have not shown (core EBIT margin about 9%), it was paid for from the balance sheet (cash CHF 139m to 26m), and the US seat goes interim to the CFO on 1 January 2027; the group's 74 is coherent, and I sit just below Instalco's working founder-led reset and above Theon's pivot.

#3 Value chain, competitive advantage, financial profile and management

Conclusion: a favourable industry structure and a real, regulation-protected niche sit on a financial profile and a governance structure that are, today, no better than average.

Industry and value chain: favourable, except at the buyer. The top four orthopaedic companies hold about 64% of trauma and extremities and compete on breadth and bundling, not price. Titanium suppliers have no leverage, and regulation raises the cost of entry. The pressure point is the buyer: about 62% of US sales sit under purchasing contracts with automatic price reductions of 1% to 3% a year, and the hospital contract, not the surgeon, often chooses the implant. Medartis is strong with the surgeon and weak with the hospital administrator.

Competitive advantage: a defended niche, not a fortress. Medartis claims more than 30% of the global market for hand and wrist fixation but has only about 2% of US upper extremities. Its strongest moat, and the one that is widening, is TOUCH. TOUCH cleared the hardest US approval route, has more than ten years of European use and holds over 70% share in well-penetrated European markets. France shows how far conversion can go: by 2024 prostheses were 75% of thumb-base operations there, and TOUCH had 85% of those. Medartis's broadest moat is training, because surgeons stay with the system they learned on. Its design lead in plating is narrowing, and it has none of the majors' scale or contract power. The addressable market of CHF 5bn to 6bn, growing 8% to 9% a year, is about 16 times Medartis's sales, so market size is not the constraint.

Upper extremities, the home of hand, wrist and TOUCH, carry almost all of the growth.

Financial profile: excellent at the top of the income statement, below average at the bottom. A core gross margin well above the majors' narrows to a return on invested capital below the cost of capital (figure below). Working capital is about 48% of sales, and free cash flow is negative. The earnings base is also cluttered: a long bridge from reported to "core" profit, CHF 4.3m a year of capitalised development cost, and currency swings on more than CHF 200m of unhedged intercompany loans.

Reported half-year profit swings widely even as revenue growth accelerates to about 30%: the cluttered earnings base in the numbers.

Management: a strong operator, a thin bench and founder control. Mr Schupp acts fast and has done what he said he would. The senior team comes from one network: the chairman, the finance director and the audit-committee expert are all ex-Straumann. The founder controls 39.9% of votes under an opting-out clause, which lets a buyer take control without bidding for the minority shareholders. Medartis pays no dividend, buys back no shares and has no internal audit function.

Inference: the margin gap to peers is a scale gap. That is the hopeful reading of a weak financial profile: profitability depends on growth continuing, and growth is the proven part.

So what. Franchise quality is high, but financial quality has to be earned between 2027 and 2029. The fair multiple in topic #11 depends on which of the two an investor chooses to capitalise.

Strongest counter-case: the clinical moat is thinner than TOUCH's market share suggests. The UK Hand Registry finds that TOUCH patients recover faster in the first six months but have no lasting advantage over the older operation (removing the bone), and face a higher risk of revision. Rival thumb prostheses already sell in Europe. TOUCH's US position is protected by time and regulation, not by uniqueness.

What would change my view. Up: returns on new capital rising as capital spending falls after 2027. Down: a US insurer or hospital system citing the registry evidence to restrict TOUCH; a major launching a bundled hand portfolio.

Against the market. The brokers' numbers describe a high-quality compounder. I agree about the franchise and about management's drive. Today's financial foundations, however, are those of a below-average business with an above-average opportunity.

47

Score: 47, set by the Rater. Qualitatively above average: a concentrated, rational, barrier-protected chain with buyer power at the hospital administrator, over 30% of global hand and wrist fixation, a widening regulation-protected TOUCH moat and surgeon training lock-in, and a fast, honest operator (groups 60, 57, 60). The financial profile drags it below typical: an 81% gross margin becomes a 9% EBIT margin, ROIC about 5% against an 8% cost of capital (2.1%, 17.8th percentile, reported), negative free cash flow, cluttered core earnings, net debt about 2.4x, low predictability of earnings and founder-first governance (group 32). It sits just below Xvivo, the closest medtech case of a real niche moat on depressed returns, which has the cleaner balance sheet, and above IMCD.

#4 Guidance conservatism, expectation management and the delivery record

Conclusion: guidance is credibly conservative on growth, capped on margin and silent on everything that decides EPS, and the delivery record matches each of the three.

Evidence.

  • Growth guidance has been raised at the half-year and beaten, two years running, and a third beat is signalled. On 2 November 2026 the company said it was "well positioned to exceed" its raised FY2026 range of 17% to 19%. Within ten months the US TOUCH projection for 2026 rose from 1,200 procedures to about 3,000 (chart below).
  • Margin guidance has never moved. The margin guide is "high teens at constant currency" every time, and the company delivers exactly that: 18.4% in FY2025 and 18.0% in H1 2026 on its own basis.
  • Nothing is guided below EBITDA. The company gives no tax rate, financial result, EPS, cash flow or mid-term target, and it reports results only twice a year.
  • The record against the sell-side splits the same way: revenue has beaten, profit has not. FY2025 core net profit was 36% below the consensus of the time, and FY2025 consensus EPS had already fallen 78% over the twelve months before the results.
  • The older record belongs to previous management: a profit warning in 2019 and a guidance cut and miss in FY2024, both before Mr Schupp arrived.

Inference: the growth range is a floor and the margin wording is a ceiling. Read literally, "high teens at constant currency" allows an EBITDA margin of about 19.5% on a reported basis. That is exactly the model's FY2027 margin, and below the two brokers' 20.1%.

Management is conservative where it guides and encouraging where it does not. Management has told analysts that tax rates above 19% are too cautious while reporting a 46% rate. The brokers' revenue sits above guidance by their own choice; their tax rate sits below the reported rate at management's prompting.

So what. The conservatism Richard looks for exists on the growth line only. A single year can be a guidance beat and an earnings miss at once, as FY2025 was.

Strongest counter-case: the finance director may extend under-promising to margin. Under-promising is the Straumann finance tradition, and Straumann raised its 2026 margin guide in June. A finance director with a cash mandate may apply the same approach to Medartis's margin from 2027, which would turn the margin ceiling into a floor.

What would change my view. A change in the margin wording on 2 March 2027 (for example "around 20%", or an explicit improvement on 2026); a stated tax rate for the year; mid-term targets, which I think about 35% likely by mid-2028.

Against the market. The brokers treat guidance as a floor for both growth and margin. I agree on growth, and disagree on margin until the wording changes.

55

Score: 55, set by the Rater. Where it guides the record is good under the new CEO: growth guidance raised at the half-year and beaten in FY2025 and FY2026 (a third beat signalled), TOUCH projections raised from 1,200 to about 3,000, and the 'high teens' margin delivered exactly. Against that, nothing is guided below EBITDA, FY2025 core net profit came in 36% below consensus after consensus EPS fell 78%, management steers brokers to a sub-19% tax rate while reporting 46%, so expectations are not kept conservative where EPS is decided (sell-side group 27 against guidance group 63). Just above CVS's targets met after earlier disappointments, below Renew's honest cut-then-beat.

#5 Does revenue growth produce outsized profit growth?

Conclusion: the business model does gear revenue into profit, but the gearing is back-loaded to 2028 to 2030 and, for the next 18 months, depends on management decisions and a tax rate, not on sales.

Evidence, lever by lever.

  • Pricing power: one product in one country. Like-for-like prices in plating are flat to slightly down. TOUCH carries a premium price in the US, and the mix shift towards TOUCH adds one to two points a year to growth until 2028.
  • Operating leverage: high in theory, modest so far, and lopsided. A contribution margin of 60% to 65% should let profit grow much faster than sales. In practice the incremental EBITDA margin has been 15% to 21.5%, while the model needs 25% in FY2027 and 27% to 29% after (chart below). Selling and distribution cost rose to 37.1% of sales in H1 2026, from 36.4%; the model needs it to fall towards 34%. The leverage is lopsided because revenue beats are reinvested, so only about 20% of extra revenue reaches EBITDA, while shortfalls drop through at 50% to 60% because the cost base for high-teens growth is already committed.
  • Financial leverage: a fixed cost that shrinks. Net financing cost of about CHF 12m a year takes 27% of operating profit in FY2027 and 15% in FY2030.
  • Cost-out: small in the plan, large as a defence. Identified savings are CHF 5m to 8m a year by FY2028, of which half is assumed to be reinvested. If growth stalled, holding discretionary growth spending flat could add three to five points of margin within two years.
  • Feedback loops: one works for revenue, one works against profit. A reinforcing loop drives US revenue: training creates TOUCH users, TOUCH accounts open the door for plates, fuller accounts keep exclusive distributors loyal, and those distributors bring more surgeons to training. A second, under-appreciated loop works against profit. The inventory and instrument sets that growth requires abroad absorb cash (about CHF 33 of working capital for each CHF 100 of new sales) and also inflate the tax rate. The tax rate rises because profit booked when the Swiss and French plants sell to the group's own subsidiaries is taxed, with no deferred tax asset recognised against it. In FY2025 that intra-group item added CHF 5.1m of tax to a theoretical charge of CHF 1.7m at the 13% Swiss rate. The same inventory build that eats the cash feeds the tax charge.
about 20%of a revenue beat reaches EBITDA (reinvested)
50% to 60%of a shortfall drops through (cost committed)
27% → 15%net financing cost as a share of operating profit, FY2027 to FY2030

Inference: on paper the gearing is strong, but it is back-loaded. Between FY2026 and FY2030 the model turns 14% a year of revenue growth into 25% a year of operating-profit growth and 35% a year of EPS growth. In FY2027, however, CHF 4.5m more depreciation and the loss of FY2026's currency gain absorb the extra gross profit. Within the 18-month window, EPS is geared to two management decisions (how much margin to release, and where to hold inventory), not to sales.

So what. The outsized profit growth Richard looks for is a 2028 to 2030 property. Buying it today means paying for it before the evidence arrives.

Strongest counter-case: close peers have not released margin while growing. Medacta, the closest model, let its margin slip from 29.5% in 2019 to 26.3% in 2023 while growing at double-digit rates, and Straumann sets itself only 0.4 to 0.5 points of margin improvement a year. Against that, Medartis starts from an 18% margin, not 28%, and making US plates in Indiana from 2027 attacks the tariff, the dollar mismatch and the tax leak with one move.

What would change my view. Up: an H2 2026 selling-cost ratio below H1's; a core tax rate under 40% for FY2026; inventory abroad growing more slowly than sales. Down: the opposite on any two of these three.

Against the market. The two brokers have the gearing arriving in FY2027, with a 22% incremental EBIT margin and a 21% tax rate. Their rate of operating leverage is defensible, but their timing is a year to eighteen months early. On tax, the brokers are simply ahead of the facts.

60

Score: 60, set by the Rater. The structure has real gearing: a 60-65% contribution margin and largely committed cost base, a shrinking fixed financing cost (27% of operating profit in FY2027, 15% in FY2030) that amplifies EPS, three to five points of defensive cost-out, and a reinforcing training-TOUCH-plates-distributor loop; the model turns 14% revenue growth into about 35% EPS growth. But it is unproven and asymmetric: incremental EBITDA margins of 15-21.5% because beats are reinvested while shortfalls drop through at 50-60%, plating price flat to down (pricing power only on TOUCH in the US), and a negative loop where the working-capital build abroad absorbs cash and inflates tax. Above the asymmetric 50s on the fixed-cost structure and financial leverage, short of the 75s where two gears are proven.

#6 Forecast financials, and the five judgements behind them

Conclusion: the forecasts show double-digit revenue growth at the rate of the past and, for the first time, margins and EPS breaking above their historical range, with EPS 20% to 37.5% below the two brokers.

The forecasts of record: the Financial Analyst's model, update 2, which I left unchanged.

FY2026 revenue growth includes about nine points from acquisitions. The model's free cash flow is stricter than cash by about CHF 4.5m a year, because it deducts non-cash financing items, mainly the accretion on the convertible bond.

What the forecasts say.

  • Revenue grows at its historical rate. Revenue compounds at about 16% a year from FY2025 to FY2030, the same rate as from FY2020 to FY2025, and every year is double-digit. Organic growth is about 19.5% to 20% in FY2026 and about 17% in FY2027, fading to 11% to 12%.
  • Everything below gross profit leaves its historical range for the first time. The EBITDA margin has sat between 15% and 19% since FY2019 and has never held above 19%; the model has it above 19% from FY2027. The operating margin rises by more than four points, and EPS more than triples between FY2026 and FY2030. Free cash flow turns positive in FY2028, as capital spending falls from 10.6% of sales to about 7.4%.
  • One driver carries the difference: US TOUCH. US TOUCH procedures rise from about 3,000 in 2026 to 7,000 in 2027 and 10,000 in 2028, lifting North America from 19% of sales in FY2025 to about 27% in FY2028.

History: revenue has grown at double digits in most years, and the margins the forecasts now exceed were never held.

Why I changed no forecast input: on the three inputs where my reading differs most from the earlier analysts', the differences offset or confirm the model.

  1. TOUCH volume has upside the model does not need. By end-2026 about 375 US surgeons will be trained (45 at reference centres plus the 330 trained in 2026), and 2027 should add about 400 more, so the average trained base in 2027 is about 575. The model's 7,000 procedures is therefore 12 per trained surgeon, or one a month, against about 14 each in 2026. The model thus assumes no deepening of use, while management expects experienced users to reach up to ten a week over five years. Volume is skewed up. The gates on TOUCH volume are hospital approvals and insurers, not surgeons' appetite.
  2. TOUCH's price is skewed down, and price matters more than volume. The model uses USD 6,500 per procedure, taken from one management remark. The chief executive's own planning figure was USD 4,000 to 4,500, and the list price is USD 8,985. At the planning figure, even 9,000 procedures in 2027 would bring less revenue than the model's 7,000 (table below). The upside on volume and the downside on price roughly offset, so I leave the revenue forecast unchanged.
  3. The "12% tax rate" in two of our research reports is a tariff rate. The report says the US tariff refund was used to bring "the rate" to about 12.5%. That statement only makes sense for the tariff the company expects on US imports, which is 12.5%. The reported core tax rate was 46% in FY2025, and 46% again in H1 2026 on twice the profit. I keep the model's tax rates of 42% for FY2026 and 35% for FY2027.

The five judgements that move the shares, with the arithmetic. In FY2027, CHF 1m of pre-tax profit is CHF 0.052 of EPS (CHF 1m, less 35% tax, over 12.45m shares). At the guideline multiple, CHF 0.10 of FY2029 EPS is worth about CHF 5.50 a share.

Judgement and the model's base If it is wrong by a plausible amount Effect on FY2027 EPS of 1.63
1a. US TOUCH volume: 7,000 procedures in 2027 Each 1,000 procedures is USD 6,500 × 0.815 = CHF 5.3m of revenue (1.6 points of group growth). At a 40% contribution that is CHF 2.1m of profit. At 5,000 procedures revenue is CHF 10.6m lower and growth is 13.4%, not 16.5% CHF 0.11 per 1,000 procedures (7%). At 5,000: -0.22, and up to -0.30 because the cost is committed. At 9,000: +0.22 if kept, about half that if reinvested
1b. US TOUCH price: USD 6,500 At USD 4,250 the 4,000 extra procedures of 2027 bring 4,000 × USD 2,250 × 0.815 = CHF 7.3m less revenue (growth 14.3%). Agents' commission falls with price; implant and support costs do not, so about 60% to 65% drops through: CHF 4.4m to 4.8m of EBITDA, and a margin of 18.7% -0.24 (15%), and a lower contribution on every later procedure
2. Growth outside TOUCH: EMEA (Europe, Middle East and Africa; 56% of sales) grows about 12% in its first year of hard comparisons Five points less growth in EMEA is CHF 197.5m × 5% = CHF 9.9m of revenue (group growth 13.6%). At a 55% drop-through that is CHF 5.4m of EBITDA and a margin of 18.6% -0.28 (17%). Five points more adds only about +0.10, because beats are reinvested
3. Margin release: EBITDA margin 19.5% in FY2027, 21.4% in FY2029 Half a point is CHF 394.3m × 0.5% = CHF 2.0m. Held at FY2026's 18.6%: CHF 3.5m less. At the brokers' 20.1%: CHF 2.4m more. Stalled at 19.5% to FY2029: 1.9 points × CHF 510.1m = CHF 9.7m less ±0.10 per half point (6%); 1.44 if held at 18.6%; 1.75 at the brokers' margin. 5. The franc: small negative bias, no hedge The realistic yearly swing on more than CHF 200m of intercompany loans is ±CHF 6m. A 10% move in the dollar is a further CHF 1.9m ±0.31 (19%) from the loans; ±0.10 from the dollar

Strongest counter-case: the brokers' bridge. No single assumption in the brokers' FY2027 EPS is absurd, but the brokers need all four of them at once (chart below): a 21% tax rate, 5% more revenue, a 0.6-point higher margin and a lower financing cost.

Consensus is two brokers, UBS and Stifel, so one change of view moves the average.

What would change my view. The FY2026 core tax charge and the margin wording on 2 March 2027, and any first disclosure of TOUCH revenue.

Against the market: the direction of the business is not in dispute, only its timing. The model agrees with the two brokers on FY2026 revenue, EBITDA, pre-tax profit and cash. It differs on FY2027 and FY2028 by 5% to 7% on revenue and by 35% to 37.5% on EPS. The brokers have the earnings arriving about a year and a half earlier than the model does.

The brokers have EPS rising far faster than revenue: that is where the model differs, by 35% to 37.5% in FY2027 and FY2028.

Conclusion: over the next 6 to 12 months guidance is likely to be upgraded and the brokers' EPS cut, and the narrative holds more unpriced awkward facts than unpriced good ones until a reset in March 2027 clears the field.

Evidence: my probabilities, event by event.

Why an FY2026 EPS miss is likely: the brokers need an implausible tax rate in H2 2026. H1 2026 core pre-tax profit was CHF 12.4m and core tax CHF 5.7m. The brokers' full-year figures leave about CHF 1.8m of tax for H2 on about CHF 13.5m of pre-tax profit: a 13% rate after 46% in H1. Nothing in our sources supports that drop. Moving the brokers' FY2027 tax rate from about 21% to about 30% would, on its own, cut their FY2027 EPS by about 12%.

Inference: guidance up and the brokers' EPS down, on the same day. Medartis will probably beat its FY2026 guidance and, in August 2027, raise its FY2027 guidance. But the model's FY2027 growth of about 17% already sits at the top of the likely first range, so a raise brings guidance up to the model's forecast, not above it. The brokers already sit above anything the company is likely to guide.

The constructive reading: a reset, then a clearer field. After March 2027 the brokers' numbers are likely to sit close to the model's, with a tax rate of 30% or more and a "high teens" margin. From that lower base, the surprises still available are mostly good ones, and nobody is discussing them:

  • a change in the margin wording, which would be this management's first signal on the strength the market most needs to see;
  • the tax rate starting to fall, as US plating moves to Indiana and loss-making subsidiaries use CHF 22.5m of unrecognised tax losses;
  • the full three-year length of TOUCH's payment window, with no rival and the approval pathway closed;
  • the company disclosing TOUCH revenue, which would let the market value TOUCH as the Bonesupport-like asset it is;
  • two technical corrections. Databases overstate the share count (14.7m against 12.45m outstanding) and the enterprise value (CHF 1,721m against about CHF 1,540m), so enterprise-value multiples are 8% to 10% lower than screens show. And conversion of the convertible bond does not dilute EPS.

The scope for upgrades is therefore negative for the next four months and neutral to positive from August 2027, when the first half-year arrives with the tariff cost gone and TOUCH wholly inside the organic base.

The awkward facts the narrative has not absorbed: the 46% tax rate and its cause; how little the US grew outside TOUCH; that part of the H2 2026 acceleration is definitional, because KeriMedical enters the organic base in July 2026; the rise in bank debt; and everything dated 2029.

Strongest counter-case: the tax rate may really fall in H2 2026. In that case, which I think 10% to 15% likely, FY2026 EPS meets the brokers' figure, revisions stay positive, and the stock moves straight into its reinforcing phase. A second counter-case: "consensus" is two people. The two brokers may choose not to cut, and a third contributor would move the average whatever the fundamentals.

What would change my view. One number: the FY2026 core tax charge, due on 2 March 2027.

Against the market. The narrative expects upgrades to continue across the board. I expect upgrades to guidance, little change to the brokers' revenue and downgrades to their EPS, followed by a better starting point.

37

Score: 37, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely beaten (85%) and raised in August (50%), with a 45% chance the margin wording moves, but the growth raise only brings guidance up to the model's ~17% and is small against 16% growth (about 0.1). Consensus EPS, the price line, is 20-37.5% above the model and 70% likely to be cut by more than 10% (a scaled downgrade of about -1 to -2), driven by a tax rate the H1 46% does not support, and the narrative holds more unpriced awkward facts (tax, US ex-TOUCH growth, debt, 2029) than good ones until the March reset. Below the group's 42 because the consensus cut is large and likely; just below IMCD's limited scope, above TT Electronics' flattered revisions.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, share price and peers

Conclusion: momentum in guidance, estimates and price is strong but company-specific, narrow and extended, and the market is already discounting the brokers' EPS on which it rests.

Evidence.

  • Sell-side momentum is strong. The brokers' FY2027 EPS is up 15% over one month and 18% over six; their EBITDA is up 9% and 12%, their sales 4% and 7%, and their target prices 12% and 32%. The dashboard's pinned sell-side earnings momentum letter is B (snapshot of 15 November 2026).
  • But sell-side momentum is narrow and shows first cracks. It rests on two brokers, who updated on 2 and 3 November 2026. The share of buy ratings fell from 100% to 75% in three months. The brokers' targets of CHF 120 and CHF 129 are only 10% and 18% above the share price: even on numbers the model judges too high, the brokers see limited upside.
  • Share-price momentum is strong and extended. The price is up 45.1% over twelve months and 16.6% over three, sits 28% above its 200-day average, and ranks in the 88th percentile of the universe for relative strength. The pinned technical momentum letter is nonetheless D.
  • The narrative is positive but thin. Our research found no broker note and no investor commentary; the company's own releases set the story.
  • Peers mostly move the other way. Of 21 sector peers (one without data), ten carry a technical letter of D or F and ten an earnings-momentum letter of D or F. Medacta is F on both (down 27.4% in a year); Smith & Nephew is D and F. The exceptions are Bonesupport (A and B, up 54.7%) and Straumann (A and A). Fifteen of the 21 peers trade below the 20th percentile of their own ten-year P/E.

Inference: the momentum is Medartis's own, and the market trusts it less than it appears. Peers explain only 6% of the daily variance of Medartis's share price. The multiple also tells a quieter story than the price. In February 2026 the stock traded on 38.8 times the brokers' two-year-forward EPS; after the March 2026 results the multiple fell to 32.1 times, and it is 32.7 times today. The whole 42% rise in the price since March has therefore come from rising estimates and the passage of time, and none of it from the multiple. Since the brokers' numbers last proved too high, the market has paid less for each franc of their EPS.

So what: the market already sits between the model and the brokers. At CHF 109 the price equals the stock's ten-year median multiple (46.6 times) on forward EPS of CHF 2.34, which is about 14% above the model's figure and about 30% below the brokers'. The market is not waiting to be told that the brokers are too high. It is waiting to learn by how much.

Strongest counter-case: momentum of this kind attracts coverage. Five houses are named as covering Medartis, and only two show in FactSet. New contributors after a strong FY2026 could extend the upgrade cycle on revenue alone.

What would change my view. Up: the multiple on the brokers' EPS recovering towards its February 2026 level, which would show trust returning. Down: a second house moving off Buy; a founder block sale.

Against the market. The dashboard's valuation letter is A and its sell-side revisions letter is B; both are readings of the brokers' estimates. I agree that momentum is strong. I think its quality is lower than its letters suggest.

80

Score: 80, set by the Rater. Both measures positive and none strongly negative gives B: growth guidance raised twice and an over-delivery signalled, brokers' FY2027 EPS +15% in one month and +18% in six (about 0.9-1.1x the 16% growth rate), targets +32%, and the price up 45% in a year and 28% above a rising 200-day average. Placed in the lower-middle of B because the sell-side reading rests on two brokers, the Buy share fell from 100% to 75%, the narrative is thin and the price is extended; peers are mostly D/F but are not comparable enough to pull it down.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the case

Conclusion: the case is simple in its drivers, concentrated in one product, wide in its earnings outcomes and thin in balance-sheet room, with precedents of 15% to 18% falls in the month of each past disappointment.

The case is simple to state and hard to forecast.

  • Simple. Everything that makes the forecast different from the past comes from four numbers: US TOUCH revenue, the selling-cost ratio, the tax rate and the depreciation ratio. The franc adds variance without changing the expected outcome.
  • Concentrated. US TOUCH is about 9% of FY2027 revenue, about 38% of that year's revenue increase and, on the earlier analyst's estimate, about 60% of its profit increase. If US TOUCH merely held its late-2026 run-rate, group growth would still be 12% to 13%: the broad base protects the top line, but not the earnings step-up.
  • Wide where it matters: EPS. The FY2027 EPS range is many times wider than the revenue range (chart below). A little more than half of the EPS range comes from tax and currency, which the company neither guides nor hedges. Even FY2026, with six weeks left, is known to about 1.5% on revenue but only to about 20% on EPS.

Trackability: good content, but only twice a year. The company discloses organic growth by region, TOUCH procedures, surgeons trained, local production and the tariff cost. It reports only at the half-year and the full year, so the range of outcomes narrows in steps, by about a third on 2 March 2027. Between results, the franc, peers' quarterly reports, Medicare rule-making and the US device databases serve as proxies.

Sudden risks exist, and each is low-probability: a TOUCH safety or revision signal; a halt at the Basel plant (a 2023 ransomware attack stopped production for a week and cost about 3% of that half-year's sales); a franc spike; a pause imposed by hospital administrators; the loss of the chief executive.

The balance sheet has no spare room. Net financial debt was already about 2.4 times trailing EBITDA at June 2026, before leases, earn-outs and the NeoOrtho buy-out, and planned borrowing would use almost all of the known bank facilities by end-2027 (figure below). The plan is fundable, but a stumble or a further acquisition would probably need new equity. And 2029 is crowded: the bondholders' put in April, the company's call from May if the shares hold above CHF 130.94, the NeoOrtho payment, and the first year after TOUCH's payment window.

When Medartis has disappointed, its shares have fallen 15% to 18% in the month. The monthly record gives three precedents: an 18% fall in the month of the August 2019 growth miss; a 15% fall in the month of the August 2024 guidance cut, and 27% within three months; and a 17% fall in the month of the March 2026 results, when revenue beat and profit missed. The earlier work said the market "looked through" that last miss. The record does not show it: the price took until October 2026 to regain its February level. Our files cannot separate the results from the wider market in that month, so I treat the March 2026 fall as a precedent for a fall of roughly a sixth to a fifth, not as proof.

Peers' first slowdowns cost a quarter to a half of the price, and only a protected product earned it back. Medacta is at the bottom of its ten-year P/E range after its growth halved. Treace fell 50% overnight in May 2024, and its sales multiple went from 12.5 times to 1.5 times. Straumann's forward P/E went from 32 to 26. Bonesupport is the hopeful case: its shares went from SEK 400 to 172 on a one-quarter US pause, and back to 321 once US sales grew 49%.

There is no sector floor under the shares. A beta of 0.49 looks like low risk. In fact it means the risk is specific to Medartis, with a sector P/E of about 17 beneath a stock on twice that. The earlier work puts a fair trough value at CHF 65 to 80 if growth stumbles.

Cyclicality is low. Trauma and hand surgery cannot be deferred, and sales fell only 1.9% in 2020. TOUCH, being elective, is the one cyclical product line.

The can-do reading: three features make the risk workable. The risks have dates. The earnings-side risks (tax, currency, margin timing) hurt the share price without harming the franchise. And management holds a defensive lever: three to five points of margin from discretionary spending if growth stalls.

Strongest counter-case: the case is safer than this section suggests. The market is non-cyclical, the European base is 56% of sales, and TOUCH has a three-year payment window. On that view the volatility of EPS is noise, and a three-year holder can ignore it.

What would change my view. Down: working capital above 46% of sales at end-2026; bank borrowing near the facility limit; selling cost above 38% of sales.

Against the market. Screens show a low-beta stock at the bottom of its valuation range. I see a stock driven by company-specific risk, on about 53 times the model's forward EPS, with a wide range of earnings outcomes.

29

Score: 29, set by the Rater. Revenue is predictable (FY2027 within about 4% either side, non-cyclical trauma base, sales -1.9% in 2020), but the FY2027 EPS cone is CHF 1.01 to 2.34, minus 38% to plus 44%, more than half from tax and currency the company neither guides nor hedges; the earnings step-up is concentrated in one product in one country at an unverified price, results come twice a year, net debt about 2.4x leaves no room (4.9x reported, 88th percentile), and each past disappointment cost 15-18% in the month. Dated, trackable and mostly non-fatal risks lift it off the floor; coherent with the groups' 34 and 42, just above Entra and below Helios Towers.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: the stock is in its broadening phase, late in the part that revenue alone can carry, with roughly 16 months to prove the earnings that a reinforcing phase requires.

Assessment: the thesis is broadening, and the hand-over from revenue to earnings is still to come. I agree with the dashboard's starting phase.

The path so far.

  • Bottoming, late 2024. After the guidance cut and miss, the shares sat at CHF 55 to 57 as the chief executive changed.
  • Turning up, 2025. A new chief executive, a reset of the US distribution channel, US approval for TOUCH, and the first raise and beat. The shares rose 56% in the year.
  • Broadening, 2026. The thesis now has more legs: TOUCH adoption ahead of plan, a second raise, a third signalled, tariffs fading, and estimates and targets rising.

Why the stock is not yet in its reinforcing phase. A reinforcing phase needs earnings to confirm the story: margin release, cash turning positive, and EPS upgrades that feed on themselves. Here the next EPS revisions are more likely down than up, the margin has never been released, and cash is still flowing out.

What decides the next phase, and when.

  • To reinforcing. A change in the margin wording and a falling tax rate would move the engine of the thesis from revenue to earnings. The earliest date is 2 March 2027; the more likely one is the August 2027 half-year.
  • To stalling. On the model's forecasts the first opening growth guide for FY2028, in March 2028, is more likely than not (about 60%) to be lower than the year before. By the sector's pattern, that is the moment the market stops paying for acceleration. If earnings delivery has not taken over by then, the phase turns to stalling.

So what: the hand-over, not the growth rate, is the lifecycle question. Medartis has about 16 months to hand the thesis from the revenue engine to the earnings engine.

Strongest counter-case: a protected product can carry a stock through a pause. Bonesupport shows that a protected product can keep a stock in its delivery phase straight through a pause. If TOUCH compounds faster than the model's 7,000 procedures in 2027, growth may not decelerate on schedule, and the hand-over to earnings can wait.

What would change my view. A step-down in growth guidance before March 2028 would mean the stalling phase has come early. A raised margin guide in March 2027 would mean the reinforcing phase has come early.

Against the market. The market's own multiple agrees more with caution than with the "broadening" label: the market pays the bottom of the ten-year range for the brokers' EPS, which is not how a stock in peak delivery is priced.

62

Score: 62, set by the Rater. The memo's Broadening is right on revenue (TOUCH ahead of plan, a second raise and a third signalled, estimates and targets rising) and the computed Stalling is too harsh, but it is late in the part revenue can carry: the next EPS revisions are more likely down at the March reset, the margin has never been released, cash still flows out, and a step-down in the opening growth guide is about 60% likely in March 2028. A broadening stock with a dated earnings stumble ahead sits below Kerry's mid-cycle Reinforcing and just above Nexans' paused momentum.

#11 The fair multiple: my view of the guideline

Conclusion: the guideline's 55.4 times is defensible only if the stock moves into its reinforcing phase, and my central view of a fair two-year-forward multiple on the model's EPS is about 45 times.

The guideline. For a stock in its broadening phase, Viewforth's guideline sets the fair two-year-forward P/E at the 80th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history: 55.4 times (the model applies 55.38). The dashboard's Phases page shows the guideline as 70% above "the multiple now" of 32.7 times.

My view: the guideline is the top of the defensible range, not its centre. I would centre a fair two-year-forward multiple for end-2027 at about 45 times the model's EPS, between the dashboard's "conservative" band (43.1 times) and the ten-year median (46.6 times). Topic #12 uses the guideline, as instructed.

The most important point: the re-rating the guideline needs is hidden inside the brokers' coming EPS cut. The 70% gap is measured against the brokers' EPS. On the model's EPS the shares already trade on 53.3 times, so the guideline asks for a rise of only 4%. Put the two together: for the guideline value to hold, the market must lift the multiple it pays on consensus EPS from about 33 to about 55 while consensus EPS falls by more than a third to the model's figures. That can happen, but it is a demanding assumption.

What supports the guideline.

  • History. The stock's median multiple is 46.6 times and its upper quartile 53.6 times, and those multiples were paid on consensus EPS that was regularly cut afterwards.
  • Earnings are still depressed in the valuation year. FY2029 EPS of CHF 3.20 carries a 26% tax rate, against management's 18% to 19%, and a financing cost of about a fifth of operating profit. At a 19% tax rate FY2029 EPS would be CHF 3.51, so 55 times the model's EPS is about 50 times a more normal figure.
  • Scarcity. A protected product in a three-year payment window is rare. Bonesupport, the only comparable situation in the sector, is also the only other sector stock on a multiple above 30.

What argues for less.

  • The market's revealed multiple. Through eight months of beats and raises the market has paid 28 to 32 times the brokers' forward EPS, not 55.
  • The guideline's own logic. The guideline allows higher multiples in peak delivery and asks for lower ones where forecasts are uncertain, and the model's FY2027 EPS range runs from minus 38% to plus 44%.
  • Normalisation. The stock's historical multiple is high because its margins were depressed. As the operating margin moves from 9% to 14% and tax falls, the multiple should compress, not hold. By FY2030, EPS growth has slowed to 28%.
  • Private-market value. Buyers paid about 4 times forward sales for Paragon 28 and 5 times for Wright Medical. At CHF 109, Medartis's corrected enterprise value is already about 4.0 times FY2027 sales (about CHF 1,590m including leases, against CHF 394m). On my arithmetic, the guideline value at end-2027 implies about 5.5 times FY2028 sales and about 27 times EBITDA. That is above what a strategic buyer has paid in the sector, and a buyer of Medartis needs the founder's consent.
  • The sector. The sector has de-rated to about 17 times, and Medacta shows where a Swiss orthopaedic grower lands when its growth halves.

When each view would be right. If the March and August 2027 results show margin release and a falling tax rate, the stock enters its reinforcing phase and the guideline is fair, perhaps conservative. If growth steps down before earnings step up, the right reference is the ten-year 10th percentile, 35.9 times.

Against the market. The dashboard reads the stock as cheap against its history. That reading holds only on the brokers' EPS: if their two-year-forward EPS fell by a third at an unchanged price, the P/E would be about 50. On the model's EPS the stock is at the upper quartile of its own range.

55

Score: 55, set by the Rater. The raw readings give B, but the cheapness is not real: it rests on brokers' EPS the memo shows 20-37.5% too high, and on the model's EPS the stock is on 53.3x, at its own upper quartile (53.6x) and above the Analyst's fair 45x, so measure 1 is neutral-to-dear and I move the letter to C (neutral on both). Placed in the lower half of C because both readings lean dear (twice the sector's 17x, above what Paragon 28 and Wright Medical buyers paid on sales), partly offset by TOUCH's scarcity and a still-depressed tax rate in the valuation year.

#12 Total shareholder return, and what drives it

Conclusion: at the guideline multiple the model returns +62.7% to end-2027 and +121.4% to mid-2029, all of it from earnings growth at a held multiple, so the 18-month return is a judgement about the multiple and the three-year return a judgement about earnings.

The model's return at the guideline multiple.

Horizon, ending Total return Annualised Value per share From dividends From the multiple From earnings
18-month column, 31 December 2027 +62.7% +54.5% CHF 177.32 0% +3.9% +56.5%
Three-year column, 30 June 2029 +121.4% +35.5% CHF 241.36 0% +3.9% +113.1%

The horizon columns are fixed from the last reported period, so the first ends about 13 months from today and the second about 2.6 years from today.

What drives the return, in plain terms.

  • Dividends and other cash returns: nothing. Medartis has never paid a dividend or bought back a share, and the model assumes none. Conversion of the convertible bond would add about 1.15m shares and remove about CHF 7m a year of cost, leaving EPS about unchanged.
  • The multiple: almost nothing. The guideline multiple (55.38 times) is 3.9% above the 53.3 times the shares trade on today, on the model's own EPS.
  • Earnings: everything. The return is the growth of two-year-forward EPS at a held multiple. Today the model's forward EPS is about CHF 2.05 (a blend of FY2027 and FY2028). At end-2027 forward EPS is FY2029's CHF 3.20, and CHF 3.20 × 55.38 = CHF 177. The mid-2029 value implies forward EPS of about CHF 4.36, part of which lies beyond the five forecast years (see the end notes).

Three-fifths of the earnings part of the return rests on strengths Medartis has yet to show. Between FY2027 and FY2029 EPS almost doubles. Roughly two-fifths of that rise comes from revenue growth, a little under a third from the operating margin, about a fifth from the falling tax rate, and the rest from the fixed financing cost shrinking against a larger profit. So about two-fifths of the return rests on the strength Medartis has demonstrated, and three-fifths on strengths it has yet to show or that follow mechanically once it does.

How the 18-month value moves with the two things that decide it (FY2029 EPS as seen at end-2027, times the multiple; change against CHF 109):

The value grid: the multiple moves the 18-month value more than the EPS forecast does.

FY2029 EPS 35.9x (ten-year 10th percentile) 46.6x (ten-year median) 55.4x (guideline)
2.63 (margin stalls at 19.5%) CHF 94 (-13%) CHF 123 (+12%) CHF 146 (+34%)
3.20 (the model) CHF 115 (+5%) CHF 149 (+37%) CHF 177 (+63%)

the model at the guideline (CHF 177, +63%). My central multiple of about 45x sits just left of the median column: CHF 138 to 149 for 43x to 47x on the model's EPS.

Three insights from the grid.

  1. Over 18 months the multiple matters more than the EPS forecast. Ten points of multiple are worth about CHF 32 a share, or 29 points of return. Across the grid, the range of multiples moves the value by about CHF 62 at the model's EPS, while the range of EPS moves it by about CHF 41 at the median multiple.
  2. At 43 to 47 times, the band around my central view, the model's EPS gives a value of about CHF 138 to 149, a return of 27% to 37%. If the market kept today's 32.7 times and the brokers' FY2029 EPS fell to the model's, the value would be about CHF 105.
  3. Time works for the holder. At mid-2029 the ten-year median multiple gives about CHF 203 (+86%, about 27% a year), and even the 10th-percentile multiple gives about CHF 156 (+44%, about 15% a year). If the earnings arrive, the three-year return survives a de-rating that would erase the 18-month return.

Strongest counter-case: by mid-2029 the market may pay less than the 10th-percentile multiple. By then TOUCH's payment window has closed, growth is slowing towards 12% and the opening guides are stepping down. A market in that mood may pay less than the 10th percentile, as it has for Medacta.

What would change my view: the two tells of 2 March 2027. A raised margin guide and a tax charge below 40% would move the realistic cell of the grid up and to the right. An unchanged margin wording and a 46% tax rate would move it down and to the left.

Against the market. The brokers' targets (CHF 120 and CHF 129) imply returns of 10% to 18%; the model at the guideline implies 63%. The difference is the multiple: the brokers capitalise high EPS at about 33 times, while the guideline capitalises lower EPS at 55 times.

82

Score: 82, set by the Rater. Weighting the memo's own grid of FY2029 EPS (2.63 / 3.20 / 3.51) and multiples (35.9x / 46.6x / 55.4x) gives a central value of about CHF 144, +30% to +33%, almost all earnings progression with no dividend; the three-year check (+86% at the median multiple, +44% even at the 10th percentile) is supportive. Placed a little below the scale's ~85 for the fat lower tail: three-fifths of the earnings rest on margin and tax not yet shown, the March EPS reset, a -13% cell at a stalled margin and the 10th-percentile multiple, and 15-18% falls at each past disappointment.

#13 Summary conclusion

The business: a rare asset, well used, inside a company whose economics have not yet improved. TOUCH is approved, paid for and unrivalled in the US until the end of 2028. The management team is fast and credible, and growth has accelerated for two years. Around TOUCH sits a company with a 9% operating margin, a 46% tax rate, negative cash flow and a balance sheet with no spare room.

The investment case: strongest on revenue and franchise, weakest on upgrades. That balance is the wrong way round for the next four months, and potentially the right way round after them. The likely order of events is a growth beat with an EPS miss on 2 March 2027, a cut to the brokers' numbers, and then, from a lower bar, a period in which the surprises still available (margin wording, tax, TOUCH volume, TOUCH disclosure) lean positive.

What I would hold on to.

  • Skew. Positive on revenue and guidance; negative on the brokers' EPS until the reset; positive on EPS after the reset, if the margin and tax tells arrive.
  • Sequence. The range of outcomes narrows on three results dates, by most on the first. The predictability of the case will itself be re-rated on 2 March 2027.
  • Horizon. The 18-month return depends on the multiple the market pays for lower, more credible EPS. The three-year return depends on the earnings, and has a cushion against a de-rating.
  • The three tells. The FY2026 core tax charge. The margin wording for FY2027. The TOUCH exit rate, and any first statement of TOUCH's price.
  • The two things nobody is watching. Who runs the US from 1 January 2027, and what Medicare pays for TOUCH from 2029.

The four memo ratings.

72

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 72, set by the Rater. Clear positive input forces on both sides (external 68: an enacted, dated, rival-free TOUCH payment window and a fast-growing niche; internal 73: a broad reset that has lifted organic growth from about 12% to about 20%) are funded and in the revenue numbers, and forecast EPS growth of about 35% a year is top-decile with the margin rising above its record. Held below the high 70s because the forces act on revenue and almost nothing yet reaches profit: the step-up is back-loaded to 2028-2030 and rests on margin release and a tax fall not yet shown, so how surely it reaches profits is the weak part.

42

Foundations' Robustness: 42, set by the Rater. Quality sits just below typical (47): a regulation-protected TOUCH niche, a strong hand-and-wrist position and a favourable chain rest on returns below the cost of capital, negative free cash flow, an unhedged franc, debt close to its facilities and founder-first governance. The delivery record (55) helps only on growth; profit has missed the sell-side badly, so unlike Judges Scientific (60) there is no cash conversion or balance sheet to carry the niche moat above the middle, and it sits between the 50 and the 25 levels.

64

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 64, set by the Rater. The case fits Demand-driven EPS Upgrader in kind, reinforced by corporate change: a regulator-created demand step-up (TOUCH), US capacity in place (Indiana) and revenue delivery proven, so the demand side is evidenced. The fit is loosened by today's problems in the business, not by timing: the demand-to-EPS conversion the setup needs is unproven (9% EBIT margin, 46% tax, cash outflow, an interim US head from January), which places it in the 60s; the brokers' coming EPS cut, which the memo cites for its C, is timing and is not counted here.

30

Case Riskiness: 30, set by the Rater. Over topic 9 (29): a few dated, trackable drivers and a robust, non-cyclical revenue base, but a minus 38% to plus 44% FY2027 EPS cone, concentration of the earnings step-up in one product in one country, a balance sheet with no spare room, twice-yearly reporting and a very high multiple on the model's EPS with 15-18% falls at each past disappointment. The franchise risks are low-probability and the earnings risks non-fatal, which keeps it just above the 25 level rather than at Judges Scientific's 20.

End notes

  • The forecasts. The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model, update 2 (the forecasts of record). I changed no forecast input; topic #6 explains why. EPS is before minority interests, which take about CHF 0.05 to 0.09 a year until the NeoOrtho buy-out, and is calculated on about 12.45m shares outstanding. Margins are the company's "core" EBITDA on IFRS net sales.
  • The two brokers. "The two brokers" are UBS and Stifel, the only contributors FactSet shows, so the memo never writes "consensus expects". Part of the gap between the brokers' figures and the model's may be a difference of reporting basis.
  • Latest results. The latest Earnings Review covers the half-year to 30 June 2026, reported on 18 August 2026.
  • The three-year return column. The mid-2029 value implies forward EPS of about CHF 4.36, part of which lies beyond the five forecast years. The Financial Analyst should confirm the FY2031 EPS behind that column.
  • Charts marked as drawn for this page take their figures from the memo text; derived figures (the TOUCH revenue matrix, percentages against the model in the FY2027 range chart) are computed from the memo's own inputs. The three charts added in copy-editing (Q3 2026 peer growth, the model's next three half-years, and return by multiple and horizon) use only figures stated in the memo.
  • Default charts and tables: history is FactSet's reported basis; consensus is FactSet (the two brokers, UBS and Stifel); Viewforth forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model, update 2. The step from the last actual year to the first forecast year can include a difference of basis.
  • Colours: history blue, the brokers (consensus) violet, Viewforth orange, peers aqua; red marks falls and risks.

Appendix: a comment from the Financial Analyst on reporting basis

Our model keeps one reporting basis for history and forecasts. The checks below suggest that consensus may use a different basis for some lines, so part of the gap between our forecasts and consensus on those lines may not be a difference of view. Nothing has been adjusted in the model.

What the checks found:

  • FY2025 earnings per share: 0.18 on the brokers' basis against 0.60 on our model's basis (-69.3%).
  • FY2025 EBITDA: 44.22 on the brokers' basis against 25.62 on our model's basis (+72.6%).
  • Consensus EBITDA for FY2026 is 64.85, +153.1% against 25.62 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves +27.1%.
  • Consensus EBIT for FY2026 is 33.66, +19702.5% against 0.17 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves +27.1%.
  • Consensus net income for FY2026 is 18.38, +147.0% against 7.44 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves +27.1%.
  • Consensus earnings per share for FY2026 is 1.55, +158.5% against 0.60 in FY2025 on our model's basis; consensus revenue moves +27.1%.

Facts in the data file that commonly explain such a gap:

  • Amortisation of acquired intangibles over the last twelve months: -7.3 before tax (-0.50 per share); our model's FY2025 history does not exclude it (its EBITA equals EBIT). Brokers' adjusted figures often exclude it.
  • Hybrid bond coupons and capitalised leases are not in the data file; check the company's reporting where relevant.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
